passage:
Monday. Abhinav pinned his week above the desk: maths and chemistry blocks, one empty evening marked "spare", and lights out at 10:30 every night, written in the same ink as the chapters.
Thursday. The team bus broke down on the way back from the away match, and he got home at nine with the maths block untouched. He looked at the chart, crossed nothing out, and wrote beside it: "Away days need a lighter plan." The maths moved to the spare evening. He was asleep by 10:40.
The following Monday. His classmate Nandini yawned through the unit test after two late nights. "How are you so calm?" she asked. "I missed a day too," Abhinav said. "I just had somewhere to put it."

qa.q: What did Abhinav write beside the chart on Thursday?
What does Abhinav's calm note on Thursday suggest about how he thinks of the missed block?
qa.a: He treats it as useful information about away days rather than a failure to feel bad about.

qa.q: Which choice in the Monday plan made Thursday easy to handle?
qa.a: Leaving one evening marked "spare" gave the missed maths somewhere to go, so no sleep was lost.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Abhinav's way of planning after the test?
qa.a: She may be curious or a little envious, since her late nights left her yawning while his slack kept him calm.

grounding: A teenager builds a spare evening and a fixed bedtime into his study plan, so a missed day becomes information rather than failure.

passage:
Nikita, put the highlighter down a minute and listen to your old aunty. When I was sixteen in Aizawl, I had my exam plan in a school notebook, every single day filled. The first time I missed a day, because rain washed out the road to the tuition centre, I cried as if I had failed the exam itself. My grandfather looked at the notebook, and he asked, "Why is there no empty page?" So I began leaving Saturday afternoons blank. When I missed a day, I asked what had got in the way instead of calling myself lazy. And I wrote "sleep" into the plan like a subject. I didn't top the class. But I didn't break, and I passed everything. So, what is your blank page?
Your Lalremsiami aunty

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami miss a day of her plan at sixteen?
qa.a: Rain washed out the road to the tuition centre.

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami feel the first time she missed a day, and why?
qa.a: She was so upset that she cried as if she had failed the exam itself, because her plan left no room for anything to go wrong.

qa.q: What changed after her grandfather's question?
qa.a: She left Saturday afternoons blank, asked what got in the way instead of calling herself lazy, and wrote sleep in like a subject.

qa.q: How might Nikita take the aunt's closing question?
qa.a: Nikita may feel gently nudged to find room for rest in their own plan, rather than feeling told off.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning as a teenager to leave slack in her plan, treat a missed day as information and count sleep as part of the plan.
